text_fidelity_a: Fire HD 8 Tablet (8" HD Display, 16 GB) - Black (Previous Generation - 8th) This was such a wonderful surprise Christmas gift from my husband! I had wanted one since my Sony E-reader broke 7+ years ago! I have been using the kindle app on my phone for years but as my age progress my eyes regress. I went from no glasses to wearing 2.0 reading glasses in just under 2 years. I'm now able to read more and turn less pages. I'm in love with my new Kindle! If there are cons they are that 1) it's not pink! Why would anything ever be made in any color other than pink? Insanity! And 2) it doesn't come with a case. It's weighty and my hands tire of holding it as I'm reading myself to sleep at night. I'm still shopping for a cover that will sit stable on my stomach in bed while I read. And lastly 3) out charges with a micro USB not a new C-type. All of my devices had already upgraded to C-type so finding a long micro in the house was a pain. And after just 1 month the cable is back to the old ways of micro cables. Loosening, falling out, ba-ding ba-ding. Ugghh why hasn't it been changed to the new C-type???? The C-type cables don't do that mess. So yeah that's a negative. But overall I'm tickled pink with my table even if it isn't pink. 😇

Kindle Paperwhite E-reader (Previous generation – 2015 release) - Black, 6" High-Resolution Display (300 ppi) with Built-in Light, Wi-Fi, Ad-Supported I had my very first Kindle way back when they first came out. One day it just stopped charging. I had read dozens of books on there, and had the wifi plus 3g version which was very convenient.

I occasionally read now on the Kindle app on my computer, as I have about 97 books in my library, with probably 15-20 still unread. I noticed on Amazon that there was a promotion...Kindles on sale for Prime members. I thought, you know, it would be nice to read those books I've put off reading because it's just not the same on my computer or phone...I think I'll get another Kindle. I researched reviews for a little while, and decided all I needed was the Paperwhite with Wi-fi. The additional cost for 3G was just not worth it to me...sure, I'd used it before when traveling with my old Kindle to buy a few books, but with a little planning I could've purchased and downloaded the books beforehand. Also, some of the reviews of the higher end Kindles did not impress me.

Anyway, I received the Kindle earlier today. It came almost fully charged, and was so easy to set up. And within minutes had books from my Kindle library loaded! I've been reading for 2 hours straight and so far I love it. I am using it on maximum brightness, sure it may take more frequent charging, but I really love how bright it is and the contrast of the words on the page. I also bought a cover for it and find it is easier to hold IMO. Pages turned with a simple finger swipe.

Hopefully this will last a very long time! I've got so many books I want to read!
text_fidelity_b: Kindle Paperwhite E-reader (Previous generation – 2015 release) - Black, 6" High-Resolution Display (300 ppi) with Built-in Light, Wi-Fi, Ad-Supported

TOZO T6 True Wireless Earbuds Bluetooth 5.3 Headphones Touch Control with Wireless Charging Case IPX8 Waterproof Stereo Earphones in-Ear Built-in Mic Headset Premium Deep Bass White (2022 Upgraded) I own the TOZO T10, and I can't say enough great things about them, but alas, I stupidly left one where the puppy could get it, and now I have one ear that still performs, but the 'button' no longer works (amazing that it didn't break).

I probably should have bought another pair of the T10s, but the T6s had pretty amazing specs, so I took a chance.

First, the pros; AMAZING sound, noise isolation, fit, and sensitive fingerprint controls (no pressing). I have over ear Bose, and Beats, and these could stand against their sound quality any day.

Now the cons: you can't roam far from the phone, computer or iPad you're connected to, or the bluetooth will drop you. In fact, if a butterfly farts in the amazon, these earbuds will drop their connection to your bluetooth device. The other stand-out con is battery life. I don't know if mine were defective, but they NEVER had the battery that I enjoyed with the T10s, and they seem to be getting worse. The case will hold a charge when stored for well over a week, but the buds last about four hours with music playing in them. If you're just wearing them at the gym for an hour or two, they're fine, but if you're wearing them to drown out office noise, you're going to be out of luck after lunch.

I am considering handing these off to one of the younger people in my family who need a spare pair to use while their primary pair is charging. If TOZO comes out with a new model, I may wait to see if the folks reviewing it have the same issues. I'm actively looking for the old T10s in the meantime.
text_fidelity_b: TOZO T6 True Wireless Earbuds Bluetooth 5.3 Headphones Touch Control with Wireless Charging Case IPX8 Waterproof Stereo Earphones in-Ear Built-in Mic Headset Premium Deep Bass White (2022 Upgraded)

text_fidelity_a:
Kindle Fire (Previous Generation - 1st) I have an iPhone and PC for all my nerdy electronic gadget needs - why do I need anything else? I really didn't want an electronic device to read from - I'm old fashioned & like carting a paper book around, holding it in one hand folded back, flipping back and forth to re-read pages if I needed. I went kicking & screaming until I realized that I don't have anymore space in the house for my favorite books! So I caved and after some extensive research, I bought a Kindle Fire and a pretty pink leather case from Amazon.com - The options were good and the price was right - and it was in color! I received it in no time flat already programed & ready to start loading it up with books. I was pleasantly surprised with the feel, weight, size and convenience of reading that I explored it's other uses too. I like that fact that I can e-mail docs to my kindle like recipe .pdfs or play games the way I do on my iPhone - Go Angry Birds. I had to wait for HBO Go negotiations for Kindle to complete in June, but now that it's here, I love it - as long as I have internet connection!

Here is what I didn't like so much about it ... maybe something to review for upgrades - next generations...

It's too easy to accidentally press the power button on the bottom end and I can't count how many times I tried to shut down while I was in the middle of something. I lost all my bookmarks to A Song of Ice and Fire once - that was bad.
The power cable connection is very tiny - seems flimsy and also is next to the power button.
And while I have WiFi at home - sometimes I get a weak to no connection (at no fault to the Kindle), it's nice to plug in to the hub to watch movies or surf the Internets.
Oh and I still need to research this, but I like to know page numbers rather than a percentage (is there a setting?)

I can overlook all that - the good out weighs the negative
text_fidelity_b: Kindle Fire (Previous Generation - 1st)

text_fidelity_a:
NEW Microsoft Surface Headphones 2 - Light Gray I'm not an audiophile, but I've tried out a good number of different earbud brands lately, all across the quality spectrum. I'm grading on a curve here.

Packaging is sufficient. A few tip sizes, quick start, instructions, and whatever is in that other manual of junk I always throw away. The earbud case is lozenge shaped and pocketable enough. No external lights, which is nice if you're charging it next to your bed, but not so much if you want to know their charge status.

They are supposed to immediately start trying to bluetooth pair with something when first opened, and appeared to be trying to do so. My Surface was unable to locate them. I even tried with a second Surface. I plugged in the case and left it to charge for 15 minutes, and then they paired fine. Overall on unboxing and setup, I'd say they're adequate, but far from exceptional.

The earbuds themselves are aggressively visible. I assume they're trying to ride the I-Pod branding success, but I'm not really feeling it. Despite looking huge, they don't feel huge. They are lightweight and comfortable. They don't feel like they are going to fall out, despite not feeling like they're crammed in the ear. Fit is unusual in that you can turn the earbud like a screw to make it tighter or looser. Sound is good. I'm giving them very low marks for appearance, and very good for fit and sound.

These use swipe style controls, which I despise. I much prefer a physical button that I can just feel that I've clicked. The controls do work as advertised, but there's enough delay that it often takes me a while of swiping my ear and waiting until it gets the message. Mostly irritating when someone tries to talk to me and I can't get it to pause for several seconds.

Range is average.

Overall, Id' say there's a bit of a brand name premium on the price compared to some other products, and I'm saying that as someone who has used Surface products as my primary computers for many years now, but they're not bad. I've definitely tried more expensive earbuds that weren't as good, but of what I've tried, I'm happiest so far with the Jabra Elite series of earbuds.
text_fidelity_b: NEW Microsoft Surface Headphones 2 - Light Gray

Detail tool: This gets into the really small opening, it has a silicone tip for larger openings, but it can be removed to get into smaller ones. I used this to clean my mice and it did a wonderful job.

I purchased this just to use as a slave to be triggered by another flash - a Yongnuo 560-II. I figured this one looked pretty similar and cost a lot less (though it's less powerful and doesn't have zooming or an LCD screen, doesn't go into sleep mode. I didn't need those things). The Yongnuo was about $60 and this one was $37 at the time.

I would should 100 shots of the same setup with the same 2 flashes -- everything the same (this was for macro - close up work). Over and over again I'd find dark frames on the Neewer TT560 side and the Yongnuo was dead on every time.

If you're shooting your nephew's 5th Birthday Party and don't care if the shots come out (why aren't you using a phone cam?), then this is OK. If you care at all, pay the $25 extra and get the Yongnuo. (Actually, Yongnuo has a 460-ii model for about $40. I haven't tried that, but I'd give it a shot before this one).

text_fidelity_a:
Kindle Fire HD 8.9", 8.9" HD display, 16 GB or 32 GB, Wi-Fi or Optional 4G LTE Wireless (Previous Generation - 2nd) As with the original Fire, the out of box experience is very nicely done. Very straightforward process of just turning it on and letting the tablet register and update itself. It took about 10 minutes (with the majority of the time waiting for an update to download) and it was ready to go. It picked up all my original Fire music and books from the cloud and most of my Fire apps. I was disappointed to see that a couple of my favorite apps (TED Talks and Play Music Videos Free) were judged not compatible with my new Fire. Hopefully updates will be coming soon.

The screen is delightful! Crisp and clear, and a marked increase in resolution versus the original Fire. Videos on the HD Fire are simply amazing.

The sound quality is also a marked improvement. While it was pretty much mandatory to hook up an external speaker for the original Fire, the new Fire puts out pretty decent sound quality all on its own. I still hook it up to external speakers (I'm partial to the Bose Companion 20) for movies and music when I'm at my desk, but it puts out more than adequate sound all on its own.

Response time is more snappy than the original Fire, and the carousel is easier to navigate (smoother scrolling). Picking up a WiFi signal seems to be better with the new fire - I'm getting all signal strength bars displayed in areas of the house where I could only get 2 or 3 bars with the original Fire.

The form factor is great for video watching. The extra screen size makes a big difference. The other huge advantage to the size is typing. It's MUCH easier to see and use the onscreen keyboard than on the original Fire. I had no problems typing without a stylus; on the original Fire a stylus is a must.

So far I don't see many misses other than a hard-to-find power button. The casing and build quality is not at the same level as an iPad, but neither is the price. I'm very pleased with the price-performance level of the HD Fire.

This is not replacing my original Fire - I'll continue to use that for most of my book reading and when I need portability. For everything else, the larger screen is well worth the additional cost.

I have a Nexus 7, the iPad 2 and an HP Touchpad and the Fire is my favorite by far. Not because either the original or this new Fire are the best in terms of build quality or speed or tech specs, but for one simple reason: the Fire makes it so incredibly easy to avail myself of entertainment and content. The tight link to the Amazon ecosystem is, for me, a huge plus - it keeps my entertainment pipeline full of things I want to read, listen to or watch with little or no effort on my part. And, best of all, a lot of that content is free through Prime.

Love it, and highly recommend.
text_fidelity_b: Kindle Fire HD 8.9", 8.9" HD display, 16 GB or 32 GB, Wi-Fi or Optional 4G LTE Wireless (Previous Generation - 2nd)

text_fidelity_a:
Portable Pocket WOWOTO Projector Android Mini Smart LED DLP Projector Although this is a very compact speaker (roughly 4.5 inches long and a little over 2 inches tall) it puts out a surprisingly decent sound - better than I expected given the price point. The treble and mid range were pretty clear, and the bass, while a bit light (unavoidable given the compact size) is more than adequate for casual listening.

Usage is very straightforward. I had zero problems pairing this with a Fire 8.9 tablet and a Nexus 7. The Bluetooth range is excellent - no dropouts even with the tablet on the far side of the room (a good 30 feet from the speaker). It also has the ability to direct connect to the sound source via a standard RCA cable.

The build quality seems solid, with nicely finished seams on the plastic case. The controls on the back (on/off, charge input and RCA in) and are clearly marked. The volume, pause, etc. controls are on the top and are very nicely done - they light up with a red light when touched. Very clear, easy to use, and attractive to boot.

It also comes with a decent carry pouch, which will come in handy to protect it from scratches when carried in a backpack. The "manual" is sparse, but is not really needed -- very easy to figure out how to use this. It comes in a sturdy box, which is good for not only storing it, but also to help prevent shipping damage. (Alas, there are also some unfortunate spelling errors on the product info printed on the box.)

My main complaint, and the reason for a loss of one star, is that it has an internal, non-removable battery. Eventually the battery will fail (e.g., not be able to retain a charge) rending the speaker useless (or requiring a constant tethering to a power source). While non-removable batteries allow for a more compact size, I'd be more than happy to trade some size for the ability to replace the battery.

That one issue aside, this is a very nice speaker for the price.
[Sample provided for review]
text_fidelity_b: Portable Pocket WOWOTO Projector Android Mini Smart LED DLP Projector

After a few days its streamer box functions all stopped working. Tried all the different ways to program it. No dice. Checked if my original Roku remote still worked? It did. New remote still works on TV, just not on Roku. Total bummer. 🤬🤬🤬🤬🤬

PSB Alpha P5 Bookshelf Speaker - Black Ash I'm not an audiophile, nor do I have fancy audio equipment to measure, compare, etc. I'm just a guy who likes music. So that that as you want. That said, not that I've finally managed to get these hookedup, I can say I"m super pleased.

The look is sleek and compact. The black will fit into any modernist style, not so much if you're more rustic/wood-based decor.

The sound is rich and clear, especially if one doesn't push volume super high. There isn't a deep low bass, but that's to be expected with bookshelf speakers so I don't consider that a flaw. You can perhaps deepen the bass a bit by moving them close to the walls/floor, but I found that muddies the sound for me. Not horribly so, but noticeably. If you're looking for chest-pulsing bass therefore, you'll want to add a sub-woofer. If you don't need that, the bass coverage is fine. Mid-range and high are good as well, without sounding tinny or hard or thin, including at high volume. Vocals are clear and what I"d call natural-sounding or smooth (I recognize those are vague). Vocals stayed true through several genres (rock, singer-songwriter, prog rock, etc). Instruments also were clear. You can pick out individual instruments on ensemble pieces for instance, classical piano comes out warm and clear and stands out within orchestral concertos. Full orchestras sound fine, maybe not as full.

For their price, these are an excellent set, better than certainly most bookshelf speakers I've owned, and I don't think worse than any I've owned. I'd call them significantly better than cheap speakers, and yeah, not as good as 3000 dollar speakers I've heard, but most of us don't have that kind of money for speakers. These are a sweet spot for sound and cost. Highly recommended
text_fidelity_b: PSB Alpha P5 Bookshelf Speaker - Black Ash

text_fidelity_a: (2011 Version) Instant Immersion French Levels 1, 2 & 3 I'm terrible at learning languages. I studied French in junior high, high school and a few years in college, but I still had trouble speaking French fluently. I went to Paris a few times and even dated a French native who criticized every word I attempted, so I gave up. Despite this history of failure, I was curious to see if this Instant Immersion French kit would work for me. The box claims that it is just as good, if not better than Rosetta Stone because they refuse to spend as much on advertising. Hmm. I have a hard time believing that advertising is a main reason why Rosetta Stone is popular. The set comes with 4 CDs and the instructions recommend starting with the Ipod audio CD, though the same sheet of instructions say that it should be used as a supplement to the software. As I sampled each disc, I found that the set is really designed less for a serious French student than for a traveler or someone visiting France on business. There is no attempt to teach grammar or language structure, like present or past tense. The lessons all stress memorization and the ability to recognize and parrot standard phrases, remember a good amount of vocabulary (though not the context to use it). I was disappointed to find that it is structured more like a Berlitz language course. Using flashcards and games to learn language is nothing new, and the Oscar Lake game included is absolutely ancient, as I remember this game from 1998. The only "new" thing about this immersion program is the fact it offers an Ipod and interactive DVD option. The interactive DVD was fun to use though the video is low-tech. Also, the quizzes didn't work that well - I had to click my DVD remote arrow buttons several times before it registered my choice. Did all this it work for me? Did my ability to pronounce words improve? So-so. While I enjoyed playing the games and had fun refreshing my memory using the interactive DVD, the kit offers no real revolutionary way to learn language. It all depends on the student and how motivated you are. In that case, I'd probably do well with Berlitz if I'd only tried harder.
text_fidelity_b: (2011 Version) Instant Immersion French Levels 1, 2 & 3

text_fidelity_a:
SAMSUNG 870 QVO SATA III SSD 2TB 2.5" Internal Solid State Drive, Upgrade Desktop PC or Laptop Memory and Storage for IT Pros, Creators, Everyday Users, MZ-77Q2T0B I was immediately suspicious of the box when I saw it.

It looked like the security tape had been lifted and then reapplied as can be seen in the photo I included with this review.

This was an item sold and shipped by Amazon.

I went online to watch unboxing videos of the same product so that I might be able to spot signs of a fake product when I opened it.

I called Amazon and verified that I could return the product for a refund even if opened and then took an unboxing video of it while on the phone with an Amazon rep.

I couldn't tell from looking at the drive or the rest of the packaging that anything was wrong with it.

I told the Amazon rep that I would check with Samsung the next next day to see if they could verify if it as an authentic Samsung serial number and as a new product.

I expressed my concern that even if it was a Samsung product that it might be used and I would never have any way of knowing. Or even if I could tell it was used after I installed it I would then be in the position of having to uninstall the drive in order to return it.

The Amazon rep told me that if anything was wrong with the product that Amazon would issue a refund without requiring me to return it if it was already installed in my computer.

Samsung verified the serial number the next day as being authentic and said that I could even tell if it had been used before as well by using their magician software program.

I thought the only way I would be able to detect if it was used was if there was old data on it left by someone else but Samsung said their software could detect if the drive had been written on before.

The catch is that that software can only be used to diagnose a drive after it has been installed internally to a direct SATA connection. Their software couldn't diagnose the drive through an HDMI connection to an external dock unfortunately.

Based on it having an authentic Samsung serial number, the assurance by Samsung that their software could detect both fake and used products and the assurance by the Amazon rep that I could receive a return-less refund if needed I went ahead and had the drive installed.

I figured the worst case scenario would be that it was a fake and/or non functional drive and I would have to take it out again immediately, the best case scenario was that it was a new and working Samsung drive and the in between scenario would be an authentic but used Samsung drive.

It turned out to be a used drive. It had been wiped and reformatted but it had been written to before.

I called Amazon back and told them the drive was verified as used and I expected a refund. At first the rep refused any refund and then said I would only receive a refund if I uninstalled the drive and sent it back.

I told them that was fine with me if they were willing to pay for both the installation and the uninstallation fees charged by a computer repair shop.

The Amazon rep of course refused either option so I directed him to get a suprivisor on the call and then played the recording of the conversation I had with the Amazon rep the day before....I got my refund immediately.

The big lesson here is to record the unboxing of any expensive items you buy, especially if the packaging looks tampered with or damaged.

Another lesson is to record your phone calls with Amazon reps or with any customer service person if you are calling up with an issue.

I learned a few things about this product and Amazon throughout this process.

These QVO Samsung drives store four bits of info per solid state cell. Most consumer SSD drives store only three and some expensive special purpose ones store just one.

These drives have a shorter life spans than three bits per cell drives and handle having large amounts of data written to them at slower speeds than three bits per cell drives. They should be cheaper as a result but often aren't.

Amazon has no way of tracking where a product comes from even if it was sold and shipped by them.

Amazon just puts all the Samsung 1TB 870 QVO drives into a bin regardless of whether or not Amazon bought them from Samsung directly themselves or they were supplied to Amazon by a third party seller.

Unless its an Amazon branded product that no one sells on Amazon but Amazon (Amazon basics, 365 Foods, etc) they have no way of knowing where it originally came from even if it is “sold and shipped by Amazon”.

Buyer beware.
text_fidelity_b: SAMSUNG 870 QVO SATA III SSD 2TB 2.5" Internal Solid State Drive, Upgrade Desktop PC or Laptop Memory and Storage for IT Pros, Creators, Everyday Users, MZ-77Q2T0B

I don't think it's notably brighter, though it is a different color. It is, however, way thinner, and has a smaller bezel. The magnets on the back are awesome for sticking it to something like a refrigerator. The stylus holder is a bit clunky, though a nice thing to have. Using the stylus as a kickstand is really weakly integrated.

If you just want to scribble some notes, or make some impermanent doodles, this is an awesome product. However, the product notes on this sales page say the following: "A free mobile app makes it easy to capture digital copies of your notes for easy sharing, editing and organizing." Yet my instruction manual makes it clear that there is NO way to transfer notes from the boogie board to any app or computer, so this claim is misleading and incorrect. The diffuser doesn't really diffuse -- you can still see all the LEDs and they are annoying bright. I would not ask my talent to stare into one of these if it were on top of my camera. It needs more diffusion. I epoxied two small clips recycled from trade show badgeholder necklaces onto the sides of the light that can hold some diffusion material.

The pink filter is obviously an admission that the LEDs put out a greenish light. The pink/magenta filter brings the light back to neutral. The top-mounted slot holds only one filter at a time.

The lights are small and very light. The attached picture shows a three-unit kit inside of a 16" x 12-1/2" x 2-1/2" case that holds the filters, lights, batteries and improved [[ASIN:B0094AS7VG BestDealUSA Multifunction Ball Head Umbrella/Flash Mount/Holder/Bracket L Stand]] so I can mount them on 5/8" stud light stands.

Lights dim easily and will be useful for accents, rim lighting or run-and-gun on-camera shooting.

text_fidelity_a:
Sony XBR75Z9F 75-Inch 4K Ultra HD Smart BRAVIA LED TV I really need to begin this review by stating that I am not much of a television watcher - up until this beast was delivered to me a few days ago, and I wanted to sit and experience it before I weighed in. There is not going to be a whole bunch of technical spiel simply because I don't know much about the mighty specs that make this thing cost a fortune, however, when I sit in front of it, I am TRANSFIXED.

I have to tear myself away from the stunning visuals, of which I tested from the mundane to my absolute favorites: regular television shows to the ones that make this a movie theater in your home - watching American Beauty WITH the commentary on so I can be ensorcelled by the teachable moments in cinematography, geeking out on Planet Earth, almost feeling the waves of water, the majestic mountains at your lap, the vivid plumage and wrinkles of parrots and elephants. The elegant clouds soaring through the sky, the dust whirling around in the desert. I am just blown away by how much these images are brought to life with the 4K HD capabilities, and for a TV at this price point the sound BETTER be amazing, which it is. Netflix and Chill will never be the same.

I come home, turn this thing on and feel like Red when he is gliding across the water to meet his dear Andy Dufresne in Shawshank Redemption. I feel like Shug Avery when her father finally welcomes her into the church with open arms. LOL!

There are smart TVs and in this case, this is a genius - once you take it out of the cocoon of careful packaging and set it up, all you have to do is enjoy your apps and Smart Home features like Alexa. Screen mirroring means you can play media right from your phone. Add the Firestick and access any show pretty much from the beginning of time. HDMI connection is a breeze. Football fans will be BLOWN AWAY by the picture quality too, as with any sport.

I don't have anything bad to say - only that I am sad that this thing is SO expensive. So to that end, WATCH OUT for generous discounts as the holidays approach. And even on sale, this TV is so damn incredible that you simply won't have to buy another one for years. Put that way, this is worth three dollars a day over the course of those years for something you will not ever experience elsewhere from Sony's top of the line. This Master's series is truly masterful.

I was fortunate enough in that this model worked perfectly for me right out of the box and was astonished to read about the other viewer's experience, and do hope that this review of a WORKING model will help. I'm looking at the cheaper Sony models for a television for my bedroom and will be watching those sales myself. I'm so thankful to have been able to receive this because I am turned on AND plugged in in a way that I really had no idea was possible!
text_fidelity_b: Sony XBR75Z9F 75-Inch 4K Ultra HD Smart BRAVIA LED TV

text_fidelity_a:
Schlage WCE100 Home Indoor Camera with Nexia Home Intelligence, White This is the best overview of the components I've seen so far:

Nexia Home Bridge (this is the key component)
Schlage touch screen deadbolt w alarm
Schlage home keypad lock
Schlage home dimmer/appliance module
Schlage home indoor camera
Schlage home outdoor camera
Trane home energy management thermostat
American Standard AccuLink((tm)) remote thermostat
Trane ComfortLink ((tm)) II Control
American Standard AccuLink((tm)) Platinum ZV control (?)
Schlage home door/window sensor
Schlage home motion sensor
Other Z-Wave sensor
Other Z-Wave thermostat
Other Z-Wave lighting device
Other Z-Wave wall switch and outlet

They might have considered making the 9V battery compartment in the "Bridge" just a little bit bigger. It's a mighty snug fit and you have to remove the battery to get the MAC ID. In fact, you have to remove the 9V battery so often it's a curiosity why the battery door is such a pain to remove and why the battery is so difficult to get out of its little bay. I was actually using a flat screwdriver to pry the battery out, it's that tight.

---

Overall, now that the camera, light dimmer and lock and installed, "enrolled" and apparently functional..? WHAT A GREAT SYSTEM!!! The components look great, they're top-quality. Now that I see everything in action (especially video of my home on my iPhone) the subscription fee seems like not such a high price to pay for what you're getting. I know that I'm going to be sorely tempted to add more cameras.

The deadbolt operates with a passcode OR with a physical key. At first I was thinking that you could lock yourself out accidentally but after examining the lock and playing with the buttons I see that is not the case.

I also understand why the light dimmer module goes so well with the indoor camera -- when it gets dark, you'd want to be able to ramp up the light enough for the camera to see! It's a temptation to put the indoor camera in one of my kids room, which is what I might have done when they were small. That would be a rude intrusion these days. So it's outside a hallway that all traffic must pass through. The field of vision nearly covers the two main doors into and out of our home, also. So I can keep an eye on who's getting home when and all that parent-of-teenagers type stuff.

Is there a controller for exterior lights? Or some kind of interface that would allow me to remotely control wired exterior lights?

The only downside to this system, aside from the kludge-y installation process, is that you will want to add more components, and they aren't cheap.

Bottom line: top-quality components, frustrating "enrollment" process -- once you get it all up and running, it's quite impressive. It's nearly worth the frustration to see it all in operation. It would be nice if you could pan-and-zoom the camera. Perhaps that will be forthcoming in another camera model.

I can't help but feel that the process of "enrolling" the components couldn't be made more simple or more streamlined.

Now to budget for an exterior camera... maybe two...

---

Now that I've seen the system in operation I grasp what the manufacturer is actually offering -- remote control of your home administered via your iPhone or iPad. Ideal for working professionals. Getting everything connected and communicating was a little effort, but it's really a beautiful system in operation. You will definitely want to add more light controls and cameras, at least I would. I wonder if there's an exterior light module? There must be. Once you see it in operation the subscription will not be an issue. You are getting more than what you're paying for.

An excellent upgrade to your home and a clever way to keep tabs on a vacation home.
text_fidelity_b: Schlage WCE100 Home Indoor Camera with Nexia Home Intelligence, White

Fujifilm FinePix J40 12.2 MP Digital Camera with 3x Optical Zoom and 3-Inch LCD (Includes 2 GB SD Memory Card) The camera is $[..]for gosh sakes! It's an amazing little piece of technology. The 3X optics and 12.2MP CMOS camera are well matched in the optical train to provide a great image for casual photos adequate for most users. It's the simplest start-up I've ever seen. The viewer LCD provides a maximum size to the package. `The manual' is 7 steps of which 4 include inserting memory, battery, charging battery and turning it on. It's `point and shoot' in the extreme.

I work in the domain of optics & imaging design. My wife has a 5 year old Fuji camera of this same genre that I've gone to some lengths to compare with Nikon and Canon in this low cost market. Without getting technical ... for the old Fuji, there are no user discernable image quality differences. The Fuji optics were superior (i.e. best objective lens light capture and transfer). Take your pick between the 3 on the backend image processing system/PC interface.

My wife has carried the 5 year old Fuji in her purse every day ... that's a technically demanding reliability challenge. Fuji can be relied on to deliver the best value for money in an image capture platform if you're designing a million dollar platform or this $69 platform. You're not paying the premium for the huge advertisement budget of Nikon and Canon when you buy Fuji. I think you just get a better camera.

I can't speak to this unit's reliability for now. A 3x optical train with autofocus, f-stop, etc mechanisms and micro motors are robust to a point. They will all fail, even the highest dollar product, if exposed to the wrong environment (g-shock, sand, salt spray, thermal shock, etc).

One reviewer mentioned software loading problems. I had absolutely no problems on a Windows 7, 64bit OS.

You can't go wrong with this device. It's an excellent camera for you or the kids or the g-kids for Xmas.
text_fidelity_b: Fujifilm FinePix J40 12.2 MP Digital Camera with 3x Optical Zoom and 3-Inch LCD (Includes 2 GB SD Memory Card)

text_fidelity_a:
Belkin 6-Outlet Surge Protector with 3-Foot Cord (Plus An Extra 6-Foot Extension Cord) I'm confused. I thought when I got this surge suppressor that the extension cord was meant to be used with it so you'd have a total of nine feet of cord if needed. Apparently, the extension cord doesn't actually fit the surge suppressor; the extension cord has three two-prong receptacles that you could plug, say, lamps and the like into, but you cannot plug the surge suppressor itself into it. The extension cord is clearly marked as being for two-wire polarized, as opposed to three-prong grounded, appliances. So that's more than a little misleading.

The surge suppressor looks heavy-duty, but you are cautioned in the packaging literature that it's not to be used with "sensitive equipment" like everything we use surge suppressors for: computers, TV, etc. You can't use it with things involving water, either, like aquariums. So what would I use it for? A blow dryer? I think not. To make it even worse, you are told to cover the receptacles on the extension cord if they are not in use. There are little plastic sliders that you're supposed to use for this purpose. But one of the sliders on the extension cord I received won't stay closed. China-cheap.

Belkin has some good products, but this one doesn't impress me very much. And the whole thing is packaged in one of those awful clamshells that you risk hurting yourself on when you take the scissors to it.
text_fidelity_b: Belkin 6-Outlet Surge Protector with 3-Foot Cord (Plus An Extra 6-Foot Extension Cord)

text_fidelity_a:
Vertiv Avocent 4-Port DisplayPort 4K Ultra HD KVM Switch (SV240D) 2nd Update: Virtiv support confirmed that the display wake-up issue described below with the MacBook Pros is a known issue with this switch's firmware. I am told they will swap out your switch with one that is updated. Unfortunately, it would seem that Amazon's stock of this item as well the 2 display version have this issue. Since this is literally the only DisplayPort KVM that even remotely works with a MacBook Pro I would suggest this is worth the trouble if you fall in that category. (I haven't gotten mine back yet but I will update this when I do to confirm it's working properly.)

I also purchased the two display version and there is a problem where it creates a "stutter" in mouse movement that makes it painful to use. Even the MacBook Pro's built-in trackpad is affected by this problem! Vertiv again said that this is a firmware issue that is known about and has been fixed in later versions so a replacement is necessary.

UPDATE: I finally ran into a case where the display wouldn't show a signal even though my MacBook behaved like the monitor was attached. The case is when the MacBook wakes up from sleep. Otherwise, it works flawlessly. Also, I discovered that a "premium UHD" DisplayPort I bought on Amazon actually created problems where there wasn't one before. (If it aint broke...). When I swapped out my no-name DP cable for the fancy new one all I accomplished was creating the same problem I just described (the problem that afflicts all display switching with cheaper KVMs) where my original no-name 4K cable worked fine (except for the sleep issue.) Therefore, if you see this problem with your MacBook and your dock or KVM, try swapping out the DP cable! It would appear that Apple's DP support over USB-C is really bad.
Original Review:
For whatever reason, the new MacBook Pro support of DisplayPort from the USB-C port is very flakey. With other high-end KVMs I found that when switching back to my MBP, nearly all KVMs - even the renowned, industry-standard Black Box KVM had problems Getting sync emulation to work reliably switched to another computer and I had to replug my display cable to get the monitor to work even though the graphics card still thought the display was connected. Even with this switch, using some DisplayPort cables had the same problem with this switch but using standard 4K cables (not the flashy woven kind) worked great. Just be careful what cables you use with your MBP and you’ll be fine. The audio and USB lock feature is also super useful.

Also, you should get a good dock if for your MBP that provides full power to the USB-C port as this makes everything work better. I have found the USB-C to DisplayCables are not very good and require resets a lot. Again, I think it’s because Apple’s doing a bad job with DisplayPort. The dock has its own conversion so DisplayPort is native at that point. The CalDigit dock is worth every penny,
text_fidelity_b: Vertiv Avocent 4-Port DisplayPort 4K Ultra HD KVM Switch (SV240D)

text_fidelity_a:
ARCTIC P402BT Bluetooth Stereo Headphones with Integrated Mic, A2DP/AVRCP, 30-Hour Playback for Tablet/Smartphone/MP3 - Black These are pretty good bluetooth headphones. They excel with regard to comfort - the ear padding is plush and they have a nice balance between grip (e.g., staying put when you move) and comfort. The headband consists of 2 plastic rods without any padding, but doesn't cause a significant comfort issue.

I had zero problems pairing these with a couple of different tablets (Android operating system and the Fire version of Android). Simple, quick and painless. The operating range is also excellent, with zero dropouts at about 20 feet and only minor dropouts at 25+ feet.

The sound quality is quite good. While these open-ear designs don't have the booming bass quality of closed designs, I found the sound quality to be very good, especially in the midrange. They are an excellent choice for movie watching since the dialogue comes through so clearly.

I like the operating controls, especially the volume switch. It's a rocker-type design, so it's very easy to use without having to look at the button - just find it by feel, and press up to increase volume and down to decrease. The multifunction button is in the middle of the rocker switch and is very easy to find by touch as well.

The overall look is very snazzy, and the build quality appears solid.

There is only a modest amount of sound isolation, but that again is an issue inherent with open-ear headphones. It does cut ambient sound reasonably well - I had no problems listening to music while on a noisy treadmill without the ambient sound interfering to any significant degree.

Misses are the volume level. These have a rather limited upper volume range. Normally I set my tablet to about the 75% level and the headphone level to close to the upper point to get a good volume that blocks out ambient noise. With these, however, I had to set the tablet sound level to 100% and the earphone level also at 100%, and I still found them a bit lacking in volume. Given the price point, the range should be better.

But other than the volume issue, no complaints. Good sound, good comfort, great range and easy-to-use controls. Well worth considering.
[Sample provided for review]
text_fidelity_b: ARCTIC P402BT Bluetooth Stereo Headphones with Integrated Mic, A2DP/AVRCP, 30-Hour Playback for Tablet/Smartphone/MP3 - Black

E EyeGrab 14'' Studio Selfie Ring Light with 94'' Tripod Stand, Adjustable 3000K-7000K Color Temperature Lighting for YTB Portrait Photo Video, Camera Phone Laptop, Black This 14-inch light ring has far exceeded my expectations. First of all, it is huge! Second, it comes with a 10-inch tabletop or floor level light ring with its own stand. Of course, there are the two remotes and an app you can use to take photos and set your light levels with.

I'm an amateur at using ring lights for my photo taking, and this one is no piece of cake to set up. The instructions are terrible for someone who is usually pretty good at following them. and the remote and app take some playing around with to figure them out. Also, the remote does not automatically pair with your phone the next time you want to use it, so you have to pair them over again. This is a bit annoying.

I have a Note 10+ with a case and it barely fits into the holder. I'm so glad it does. The whole setup feels nice and sturdy all the way around, from the bottom of the stand to phone holders. I sell bulk bought makeup online, and it's nice to have a ring big enough that it doesn't show up on the surface of the shiny palettes. I can place it so there are no shadows or bright spots, and the light is up far enough that it is not in my way. It is that big. I am working with four to six inch items, so that helps, too. It makes my life so much easier.

The ten inch ring light is great for getting perfect shoe photos. I love buying shoes, and always take photos to put on the end of the boxes, so I can see exactly what I have at a glance. It makes picking out my shoes for the day easy, when I can see the actual shoe, and not a drawing of it.

These lights are the best I've bought. They are made very well, and so is everything they come with. You will not find a better setup at a better cost. A beginner or novice will have everything you need to start taking photos or videos right out of the box. You may, however, find better instructions on how to put a setup together in a different set, but then you wouldn't get half the amount or half the quality of the items you get in this one. It may take some trial and error, but if I can figure out how to set this up, I'm pretty sure anyone can. I have cognitive difficulties and things don't come easy. It took me a good while and I did ask for some help with one thing from my son, but I got it done, and it was worth the trouble. 4 stars ✨

Wacom Intuos Small Bluetooth Graphics Drawing Tablet, 4 Customizable ExpressKeys, Portable for Teachers, Students and Creators, Compatible with Chromebook Mac OS Android and Windows - Black I love this little tablet. It's an inexpensive way to sketch: Particularly if you get the pistachio, which was $20 less then the boring black one when I bought it. ¯\_(ツ)_/¯

I particularly like that it works with Android (at least on phones that support USB OTG, which is most these days). It would have been even better if the Bluetooth worked with Android, but at least with my Pixel 4, it didn't.

It doesn't come with any Android software, but Autodesk Sketchbook is free, and it's quite full of features. Sketchbook also runs on Windows 10.

SUPCASE Galaxy Tab S3 9.7" Case Unicorn Beetle Pro Series Full-Body Rugged with Built-in Screen Protector, Blue/Black (SUP-Galaxy-TabS3-9.7-UBPro-Blue/Black) When I ordered this, I didn't realize that I would be required to use the screen protector part of it. I thought that I could just slip on the back piece and use it like that. When I realized that both pieces are required (the back is too big and wouldn't stay on without the screen protector piece; hey, it's the first time I've ordered something with an integrated screen protector, so I didn't know), I wanted to send it back without even trying it.

I'm glad that I decided to try it for a couple of days, first. The screen is always covered with fingerprints and smudges and I find myself wiping it off many times a day. It also scratches easily. Since we're all washing our hands 40 times a day, the amount of fingerprints feels excessive to me and I hate looking at it. Even so, with the screen protector on, the screen is very responsive. Zero problems. And while I'm actually using my tablet, I don't notice the scratches or fingerprints.

There is also a shimmery rainbow effect. I don't really notice it while the screen is on and it seems to be less of an effect after the couple of weeks that I've been using it. I think because there's less of an air gap.

Everything lines up perfectly and the back part of the case also seems perfect to me. I would love to see this brand make a version that's just the well-fitted back piece.

So is it perfect? No. However, the things that bother me about it aren't really noticeable while the screen is on and I'm using it. It's protective and the screen protector doesn't interfere in the responsiveness of the screen in any way. So overall, I do think that this purchase was worth it. I'm glad that I decided to try it instead of immediately sending it back.

Another comment -- I keep a little piece of electrical tape over the front camera hole. The screen protector holds the tape in place so that I don't have to periodically change it anymore.
text_fidelity_b: SUPCASE Galaxy Tab S3 9.7" Case Unicorn Beetle Pro Series Full-Body Rugged with Built-in Screen Protector, Blue/Black (SUP-Galaxy-TabS3-9.7-UBPro-Blue/Black)

Not as much detail as from a bigger heavier headphone, but this is fine for listening to MP3s on my cellphone when I'm jogging. The lightweight construction means it doesn't fall out of my ears as often as heavier earbuds. I have tried some of the other cheap bluetooth headphones from Amazon, and this is the best that I have used for under $10. It even uses one of the newer Bluetooth standards that shows headphone power level on my phone screen; as someone who is always worried about rechargeable devices running out of power, this is a really great feature. Unfortunately, battery life is somewhat less than the advertised 5 hours. Even at moderate volumes, I'm down to about 50% battery after an hour and a half. That's fine for a gym workout or a subway commute, but not for airline travel.

It comes packaged in a self-destructing pile of paper and plastic. I wish they had included a carrying case instead of all this garbage.

text_fidelity_a:
Kindle Fire HDX 7", HDX Display, Wi-Fi and 4G LTE, 16 GB - Includes Special Offers (Previous Generation - 3rd) I love it! This is a replacement for my Nook HD. I think it's still useful and I still like it, but I wanted something with better specs. After some research, I chose the Kindle HDX. I like that it's built right in to be able to download from 3rd party - something that isn't easily done on a Nook. I love how the reader learns your reading speed and tells you how long it will take you to read each chapter or finish the book (Nook doesn't have it).

I considered Nexus or other pure android tablets, but Fires have better specs and for a cheaper price, with ad support. There is some bloatware, but it's minimal. I don't have to have Facebook and Twitter taking up space if I don't want them to.

In my opinion, the only con is not being able to use googleplay natively. Most things that you can get from google play, the amazon app store has an alternative or you can get an apk from elsewhere. However, I paid for AVG for tablets through googleplay, but can't use it now unless I pay for it again. The tablet game I play (Legion of Heroes) isn't in the app store yet (though it's coming). For right now, I can play my googleplay movies on my Fire, but when I sell or give away my Nook, will I still be able to access my content?

There are workarounds to get some google play stuff to work without rooting, but not paid apps and not in game purchases. You can't link your Fire to the googleplay store so if it's your only device, you're out of luck.

Fire would be the best all around tablet, if amazon and google play would learn to play nicely with each other and share. Still, I highly recommend Fire HDX
text_fidelity_b: Kindle Fire HDX 7", HDX Display, Wi-Fi and 4G LTE, 16 GB - Includes Special Offers (Previous Generation - 3rd)

Powered USB Hub Rosonway 16 Ports 100W USB 3.0 Data Hub Aluminum USB Hub 3.0 Splitter with 12V/8.3A UL Certified Power Adapter and Individual On/Off Switches RSH-A16 (Black) I haven't yet used it to its full potential. The maximum ports I've used at one time was 5, but it worked well. I've heard others say it gets hot, which may be true if it is full and all in use, but so far, it has worked fine for me.

Speed seems to be consistent with USB 3 ports. It actually seems to be limited by the external drives I was using. I've been trying to go through my old 2.0 backup drives to make sure they are backed up on newer drives after I lost a number of older drives recently. These drives were expectedly slower than my newer drives. I eventually want to turn my computer into something of a backup server, including videos and other large files, so this will come in really handy.

I also like that you can turn on and off the power to drives as they are needed, by pushing an on/off button for each port, or you can leave them all on if needed. Because it is powered, it does not turn off power to the ports if the computer is restarted. For my use, it is perfect.

Update 7/20/22
Running 4 external drives on it has it very hot. Makes me a little nervous. The area under it is not very hot. It is currently sitting on carpet that can handle a bit of heat. And actually the base isn't too hot, just the sides. I've been running recovery of hard drives and backups using it and it has been in pretty steady use for a few days. I don't think I would recommend this in any environment where your computer is constantly on.
text_fidelity_b: Powered USB Hub Rosonway 16 Ports 100W USB 3.0 Data Hub Aluminum USB Hub 3.0 Splitter with 12V/8.3A UL Certified Power Adapter and Individual On/Off Switches RSH-A16 (Black)

text_fidelity_a:
Nikon D3100 DSLR Camera with 18-55mm f/3.5-5.6 Auto Focus-S Nikkor Zoom Lens (Discontinued by Manufacturer) First, let me preface that I in NO way count myself a photog. I am just a shutter bug who has been firing frames almost non-stop since the age of 18. I learned on my dad's 'old' Nikon SLR with an f/1.2 lens. The Nikon SLRs/DSLRs I have owned are: N50, N60, N55, N80 and D50. My N50 ad N80 had the best lenses. The N60 and N55 were not as great and the D50 was a fabulous entry-level digital. The only medium format camera I own is my Holga. But hey, unlike the photographer at Portrait Innovations, at least I know 'medium format' does not refer to the number of megapixels at which I am shooting. As for my working knowledge, I had three semesters of photography in college. I can process/print both B&W and color film. (Not that that does me any good these days LOL) I can shoot completely 'manual' and I have stood among many pro photographers on the bridge at sunset, waiting for the color to be just right on Half Dome. (My Bogen tripod was way too heavy to be practical for an amateur but it gave me street credit.) So, in a nut shell, I shoot by the 'Sunny 16' rule. I know that opening my f-stop should increase my shutter speed give me a shorter depth of field; and, per the great Ansel Adams, f/8 is a proper exposure for all pictures.

That said, I hate my D3100.

I have had metering issues since I opened the box. I bought the camera so I could take 'even better' pictures of my infant son than I was getting from my D50. Ha. Joke was on me.

The contrast was BLINDING on the factory settings and every shot was over exposed. I have tried every metering option in the menu but the only changes I can achieve are under-exposure, blurred focus and missed shots. It's go high or go without.

I always lower my ISO to 100 when I'm outside because I crave rich color but it's just not there. I have tried Aperture Priority, Shutter Priority and Manual. Nothing. f/16 over my film speed on a sunny day. That's supposed to work! I have used it on many a 'less complicated' camera and achieved photos that make jaws drop. Well, there's no jaw dropping with this camera.

The metering overrides my manual choices every time. It's like I'm having a battle of wits with my camera. :( It reminds me of the days when Kodak was marketing 800-speed film as a universal, never-miss-a-shot solution to all your photo woes. Bleh. Just because there's always an image doesn't mean it's the RIGHT exposure.

I get that being an entry-level/made-for-the-masses DSLR really does mean it's a glorified point-and-shoot but it should preform at least as well as it's predecessors. Honestly, I got far more reliable results from my Canon SureShot and a roll of Kodak 100.

My expectation for a camera is that the image should be very close to perfect when the shutter closes. I know there's always room for improvement before printing but that's the art of photography. The hours I spend working on my photos after the shot should be to make them pop. Instead, my time is spent trying to rescue precious memories.

If you are considering this camera as your first DSLR because you think it will improve your skills, skip it. Invest in an equally expensive point-and-shoot that will give you all the same manual controls and preform much better in low-light situations. The D3100 does not live up to the standards of a Nikon SLR.

I gave it a second star because my son pulled mine off the counter about a year after I bought it and although the case cracked, it didn't seem to hurt the camera. Unfortunately, it impact didn't help it, either. (Yes, I was actually hopeful.)
text_fidelity_b: Nikon D3100 DSLR Camera with 18-55mm f/3.5-5.6 Auto Focus-S Nikkor Zoom Lens (Discontinued by Manufacturer)

text_fidelity_a:
SanDisk Sansa Fuze 4 GB Video MP3 Player (Black) SanDisk has come out with an extension to their array of MP3 players, beyond the Clip and the View. Their new mp3 player, the Sansa Fuze, is definitely geared towards casual someone who just wants a basic, functional, and well-put together media device for their pocket.

The Sansa Fuze may look like a tiny device at first, but this thing packs some serious features. It has the ability to playback music, video, photos, FM radio, as well as audiobooks. The features for the Sansa Fuze are very impressive to say the least, as it also features a microSD card slot to add extra storage space, content, etc.

The first feature we will focus on is the one which will likely get the most use, the audio aspect. The music menu is organized with artist, album, song, genre, etc. There is also a recently added section which shows the most recent songs added onto the device, as well as a top rated section.

The album menu allows you to see album icons as you are scrolling through the various albums. There is also the ability to form a playlist directly on the player.

The sound quality is very well-done. If you have a great set of headphones you will not be disappointed in the least bit.

The video aspect is definitely not the highlight of the Sansa Fuze. Part of this is due to the low power of the device, and partly due to the screen itself. The supplied Sansa Media Converter does make it easy to convert movies into a format for the device though. A typical movie will take up a little under, or over 1GB. The video looks respectable, but can get a bit choppy at times. One very cool feature about the video is the ability to add a bookmark while watching it.

The photo viewer is very standard as you can view photos from the internal memory of a microSD card. You can set up a slide show with time intervals, and add music as well. The images looked quite sharp.

The FM radio feature is done extremely well on the Sansa Fuze. You get some great reception and the auto program feature picks out crystal clear radio stations. It also has the ability to record radio in WAV format.

This works with voice recording as well thanks to a microphone located right below the microSD slot.

Podcasts and audiobooks are pretty self-explanatory, but one issue with the audiobooks is the lack of a bookmark feature.

The overall user interface for the Sansa Fuze is put together nicely, set up in such a way that a first-time user could pick up this device and feel right at home with it. You have a scroll wheel as well as a home button and a middle click wheel. The scroll wheel can also be clicked up and down, which can make things a bit confusing at times. Overall though, beyond a few hiccups with organizational aspects of the UI, this is one easy device to use.

Getting media onto the Sansa Fuze is extremely simple as you can use any desktop media player to create playlists and such, easily syncing them to the device. It also supports drag and drop without the need for any software. We used Windows Media Player as well as a few other media players to test this all out, and syncing was as simple as can be.

The quality of the device itself is top-notch, as the screen can put out some great contrast and vibrant colors in spots. The screen is extremely clear and does a nice job with photo presentations. Battery life is equally as impressive, as I have been getting around 20 hours on each battery charge thus far. Video playback came in at around 6 hours on a charge.

The package comes with a proprietary USB cable and a pair of earbuds, pretty basic.

Also shipping with the Sansa Fuze is a great bonus, a microSD card which comes with DRM-free music from more than 50 new and emerging artists. This is a great way to immediately test out the music capabilities of the Sansa Fuze, and also adds value to the entire package. Music videos, images, and more are also included on the microSD card.

Overall SanDisk has done a great job with the Sansa Fuze.
text_fidelity_b: SanDisk Sansa Fuze 4 GB Video MP3 Player (Black)

text_fidelity_a:
Lexar JumpDrive S35 64GB USB 3.0 Flash Drive - LJDS35-64GABNL (Assorted colors) The Lexar jump drive was the speediest drive I have, but it does feel a little more cheaply made than some. Some specifics:

I used a Macbook Pro, mid 2012
I copied over a folder with 3000 items in it, a mix of file types including video, photos, presentations, docs, PDFs, Final Draft, spreadsheets
This Lexar copied the files over in just under 5 minutes
An older Lexar USB 3.0 took exactly 8 minutes
A Transcend 3.0 took about 8.5 minutes
A Sandisk 2.0 took much longer. In the same time this Lexar took to fully copy the folder, the 2.0 Sandisk was less than a third of the way through

I did a bit more copying of fewer files and the results were consistent--this one was faster on a regular basis

Formatting for my Mac was fast and simple.

It comes with a 2-inch lanyard to attach to a key chain or whatever.

My single concern is build quality. It is plastic, like most of my flash drives, but it feels less sturdy, a bit more cheaply made. And it seems particularly thin at the outlet end (where the USB prong exits). If it breaks I'll update.

So far then, the speed is a definite plus. It's the fastest of my 3.0 flash drives. And certainly anyone with a 2.0 will want to upgrade--the difference, assuming you can take advantage of it, is hugely significant. Just that build quality to be worried about, but so far so good
text_fidelity_b: Lexar JumpDrive S35 64GB USB 3.0 Flash Drive - LJDS35-64GABNL (Assorted colors)

Over 3TBs of stuff lost; much of it irreplaceable.

If it's still working with no further issues in another year, I'll upgrade my review again.

Apple Lightning to USB Cable (2 m) IMO Apple cords still seem to work the best for Apple products. I really like the added length of this 2M cord (6.6'). I have tried many other cords that seem to work for a while, but always seem to fail sooner than Apple cords. My only complaints w/Apple cords are they are more expensive than after market cords and seem to be more fragile, particularly near the Lightening connector end. But, they do work until they literally break. I've had cords where the sheath is torn away and the inside wires are all hanging out, but as long they are connected the cable will charge. To remedy this problem, I have put CableCollars on all of my Apple cords to help reinforce the ends. This is something I wish Apple would do at the manufacturer. For Apple products, I definitely recommend Apple cords.

Update 5Aug2020: My 2m Apple iPhone charging cord is still holding up and working fine. I also just purchased a .5m cord to use on my motorcycle where I only needed a short cord to keep my iPhone charged. I like that it is an Apple cord and came in an Apple box.
text_fidelity_b: Apple Lightning to USB Cable (2 m)

And the cutouts for the buttons never look very nice or are as exact and perfect as you'd really like them to be.

That said, this one looks pretty good for one of this type, and is of good quality. Honestly, the (current) Amazon picture doesn't really do it justice. Mine is grey and the stand doesn't really work in the way the picture would have you believe. The stand does work surprisingly well (through friction). The case is soft, the top layer is perforated, and has a nice feel to it (almost like microfiber of some sort). Surprisingly, it has an integrated strap to keep it closed, which stays out of the way nicely when not in use. It's hardly needed, but might be useful if you're prone to tossing this in a bag with a bunch of books.

Again, I'm just not a huge fan of this style over the harder, more symbiotic type, but this is definitely a nice, quality case if this is the style you wish for.

Otherwise, it would have scared the %$%@ out of me, thinking someone was near the door or trying to break in. I could see there was no one there, nor had there been when it first went off. text_fidelity_a:
Sony ICFC218 Dream Machine Clock Radio (Black) This is not a bad clock radio for the price I paid. It's not a great one either, but it fit the profile of what I wanted with one exception, which I'll get to in a bit.

First off, it's smallish, which is a blessing on a crowded nightstand. The display seems fine to me, neither too bright, nor too dim. It's easy to program, thank goodness. I've had a lot of electronics that require three hands, and a stopwatch to be properly programmed. The ICF-C218 has a button or a dial for each function. Just follow the instructions and you'll be fine. It's a bit hard to see the radio dial unless you pick it up, but that's a minor thing for someone like me, who pretty much keeps it on one station. It's not programmable; you have to change the station with a tuning dial. However the reception is excellent, even without an external antenna.

My quibble, and it's a relatively small one, is that the sound is tinny. I don't expect a lot out of a small radio like this, but I have a Sangean which is even smaller, and the sound is much better. It's not a deal-breaker, I got what I wanted in every other respect.

Bottom line: Good price point for a basic clock radio with excellent reception, and so-so sound.
text_fidelity_b: Sony ICFC218 Dream Machine Clock Radio (Black)

I was looking for a MAC time machine backup drive and noticed the external drives labeled as MAC were $10 - $15 more. I then read the Q&A on this drive and someone gave the most perfect instructions:

"right out of the box it's not Mac ready, but the solution is real easy. You go to Utilities and open up Disk Utility. With the drive plugged in, select it and go to the Erase tab and there should be a drop down menu with Format. Select Mac OS and click erase and after that's done, the drive should be formatted for Mac and you can save to your heart's content."

I might only add where to find Disk Utility in case you didn't know ... in finder go to the applications folder and in that folder is utilities and in that folder is disk utility.

I did just as the person in Q&A said and the second it was done reformatting a box came up asking if I wanted to use this drive as a time machine backup drive. I said yes, and within 107 seconds I was done. Color me impressed!

We got the 1tb drive because we have a 1tb 21.5" iMac from Nov 2013.

I hope this helps someone. I will update this review later as to longevity of the drive.

UPDATE: May 6, 2018
7 months later and this little backup drive does what it should do. We have never needed to utilize the files it stores, but it is nice to know the files are there. I periodically check to make sure my Mac is recording on this drive and it functions perfectly as a time machine drive.

KINESIS Freestyle2 USB Keyboard for Mac (9" Standard Separation), Black Overall this keyboard is great. The keys feel nice and they're quiet but not too quiet or soft or squishy. Enjoy typing on this keyboard, pushing the keys seems to take minimal effort and overall it's great.

The best part about the keyboard is that it separates and having the ability to give it a little separation is great. I miss it when I don't have it and it helps avoid torquing the wrists when you are typing. I also love the feel of the keys.

Now before my minor complaints understand two things: (1) I really like this keyboard and despite what I would consider minor defects, I would definitely buy another one. (2) please excuse the fact that I like my keyboards to be consistent and while Apple may not make the *best* keyboards I do use a laptop and I am used to their keyboard layout and feel.

The biggest thing that annoyed me when I purchased this keyboard was the positioning of the ⌘ (command) key. It seems to be shifted over a bit from what I'm used to. Normally I would hit ⌘ with my thumb but it's a little touch to do that on this one given the position of it. It's just something I'm having to get used to.

One minor downside to the keyboard is that the function key doesn't work the same way as the default apple keyboard, rather, the `fn` key is a toggle. I prefer for fn to work as a modifier because that is what I am used to on my laptop keyboard.

Another minor problem is the styling on the caps lock key. Like many people, I remap my caps lock to ctrl and and thus want caps lock to be a normal button. However, on this keyboard the caps lock key is missing the right part of the key so that you don't accidentally hit it when typing the `a` key.

Finally, the escape key and '`' (back tick) keys are in weird positions. The escape key is not as bad as the backtick. There is just something about the distance that I must go that is different from what I'm used to and I have been consistently hitting the `1` key instead. Life goes on.
text_fidelity_b: KINESIS Freestyle2 USB Keyboard for Mac (9" Standard Separation), Black

HAOHUNT Camcorder Digital Video Camera HD 1080P 30fps 3.0 INCH Touch Screen 24MP Camcorder with Microphone and Wide Angle Lens Vlogging Camera with Remote Control Infrared Night Vision Recorder I am impressed right off the bat with just how many useful accessories are included right off the bat. The description says it does not come with an SD card or AAA batteries, but mine did, perhaps for review purposes, although the box did not look like it had been opened. Seems like it would come with that stuff, so perhaps other reviewers might clarify. There is a case and two separate pouches for the wider camera lens and the microphone.

Functionality and video quality are pretty good. I guess the only drawback is that this almost seems like a throwback now. For still pictures - on a vacation or a great hike where I want to take great pictures - I still take along a small camera instead of just my cell phone, but the truth is cell phone cameras are getting so good now that I wonder when that will no longer seem prudent. And with that said, my small camera takes such amazing (not studio quality) HD that I wonder when something like this would really seem like the best thing, especially considering they both take SD cards and length is only limited by SD card capacity.

It certainly does seem like a more professional camera in its size and shape, but mostly because that style has been the trend for some time now. But in a way this style is already starting to seem outdated, like a throwback. I also noticed, just now, that even the really big name manufacturers have this style in 1080p for comparable prices.

I'd definitely give this thing a look. I would have totally loved it a few years ago. The mic and extra lens still feel like premium features, but I'm rarely the one to set up for photos and video footage, as I usually just do landscapes or great spontaneous moments. This may be a fantastic alternative to giving kids your phone - or a phone - to play with. Seems like a good way to encourage their inner photographer without it leading into a bunch of cheap phone games.

Camera has mini* USB and HDMI ports (as opposed to micro) - just when I was wondering what I'd ever do with this one mini-HDMI cable I have... Mic takes 2xCR2032 batteries, which are included, and should probably last, as I don't think mics eat up much power. Has a curled, springy, analogue audio cable with stereo mini-plugs on both ends to connect the mic. Also has an external battery charger.

text_fidelity_a:
Archos 9 PC Windows 7 Starter Tablet (Black) Once calibrated, this PC tablet works wonderfully. It is responsive to the stowable stylus or a tap of my fingernail, and I can even scroll with my thumb after adjusting the right edge width. The screen is sharp and clear, and it's speedy enough for pleasurable surfing and blog-reading, which is what I mostly want to use it for. I have not watched any HD movies on it yet, although the sample movie clip included with the computer shows what it's capable of...and it's gorgeous.

But I have a problem with the Archos 9. Because there is no fan, which makes for a very quiet experience, the lithium battery does get hot when held in your hands. Now, maybe there are people who will use this computer by pulling out the little easel-like stick in the back, but not me. I want to curl up on the sofa with it like a book. So I could see immediately that I wanted to rotate my Archos 9 PC Tablet's screen to portrait orientation so the battery would be at the top and not bother me so much. Well, doing so was a BIG mistake. Once you rotate the screen, it's pretty much impossible to recalibrate it; trying to move the cursor is like trying to walk without an inner ear: Directions ceased to make sense and I'd skew off East (or was it West?) when I meant to move North. It was all I could do to manage to restore the computer to its earlier state.

The little end piece of the easel-like appendage pulled off and I had to super-glue it back on, but that wasn't such a big deal. This appendage also stows into the back of the computer, and it can be pulled out short or long depending on whether you are watching a movie or trying to type on the on-screen keyboard. I can see it for watching a movie, but there's no way I'd ever try to type on the on-screen keyboard. Hunt-and-peck with the stylus is quicker. Needless to say, I will reach for my laptop if I have to do much typing.

I installed Skype, but it was too slow to show video unless I stopped everything else from running. This is fine with me, however, because I prefer to use Skype without the visuals. Google Chrome runs very well on it. I found I preferred the software keyboard (which you can drag around the screen) to the one that pops up when you press the keyboard key. I found that by keeping the former loaded and minimized to the tray, I can get around and do things online pretty efficiently. I just wish that battery didn't get so hot OR that I could easily/reliably rotate the screen to portrait. I gave this computer four stars because, on the whole, it's quite nice. But I must say that I am not likely to reach for the Archos 9 very often because of the discomfort from the battery heat when holding it in my hands. If they will come out with a software upgrade that will make screen rotation practical, then I will be a lot happier with this tablet PC.

A word to the wise: Immediately when you take your Archos 9 out of the box and get the software installed, you need to back it up. Don't wait a second longer than you have to. I was able to restore mine to its pristine newly installed state, but had I not backed it up, the whole thing would have been trashed by my little screen rotation exploit. You don't have a restore disk with this product. So be careful.
text_fidelity_b: Archos 9 PC Windows 7 Starter Tablet (Black)

text_fidelity_a:
Shure SRH145m+ Portable Collapsible Headphones with Remote + Microphone Compatible with All Apple iOS Devices Update after 4 months

They have got more comfortable. I don't use them often so I don't think it's my ears that have got used to them I think the material has gotten softer with use and maybe the band has stretched out a bit.

I'll add to my review that while these are not hard to drive they are not easy to drive either. They are near the top of easy to drive. They are 32 ohms and sensitivity is 96db. What does that mean? I use these mostly with my computer that has a pretty good sound chip and I find that I have to have the computer sound (windows 7) and the music app (foobar 2000) volume all the way up to get these to where they open up and sound best. In general, they need to be a little louder than I would like to sound their best.

Sound wise I find myself punching up the bass a bit. They need a little bit more hit and a touch of bloom for things like the bass guitar and kik drum to sound about right. Not a lot, just a 3db boost from about 80 to 200hz. I also find they need a bit of a push at 10K and up to put a little more air around the instruments. With more listening, I'm not quite as thrilled with the sound as I was, but I still like them. Hours of listing do not leave me with ear fatigue and they do not punish poorly recorded music.

Update after a month:
These have not got more comfortable and I kinda wish I had returned them but for $32 it's not really worth it given I'd get charged $5 for the return. These hurt after a couple of hours and no amount of moving them around relieves it. The material is soft enough but I think it is too soft and packs down. Also clamping pressure is pretty high on my melon so now that I'm keeping them I may try to stretch them out a bit

================================================================

I am FUSSY about sound! I want natural neutral sound. That's what you get with these. The bass is natural, drums sound pretty good. Sibilance is there but not annoying. They are accurate without being clinical or fatiguing. They are musical without being over warm or polite. They do not punish poorly recorded music like some more HiFi headphones do. There is a nice amount of 'air' around the instruments but not much of a sound stage beyond that. They are a nice middle of the road set of headphone, not too bright, but bright enough, a good mid-range, pretty well-controlled bass without much bleed and some bass extension. They could use a touch more bloom to suit my tastes but what is there suits me fine. If I thought they were bass shy I would tell you.

I use a 15 band equalizer on my computer and I end up putting some EQ on most headphones I use, but I found with these I liked them best with no EQ. They do not go super loud with my phone. Loud enough for me, but not might be loud enough if you like your music really loud.They need a little volume to sound there best but that's pretty typical and I have had headphones that needed to be louder to sound their best.

They have one big problem. They are not very comfortable. I would not get these if wearing them all day at work is your thing of if comfort is really important to you because you get annoyed if they are not comfortable. In comparison, the Sennheiser HD 2.20 is WAY more comfortable. The foam is too thin and you almost feel like the plastic is pressed against your ears. They 2nd day they felt a little better. My ears getting used to them, or maybe the foam adapting to the shape of my ears or a little bit of both.The headband cushion is also really thin but did not bother me as much as the earpieces.

They have almost no isolation. My old open back Sennheiser 239 had more isolation. I'm also not a fan of how round that headband is but I guess they did that so they would fold up smaller? I don't know but I wish the fit a little closer to the head on the sides.

The cable is kind of weird in that the right and left cords are side by side like lamp cord and a little thicker than on other budget headphones.

Between my old Senn 239, and the Senn 2.20 and the Jabra Move (I think it was the Move) I like the sound of these Shure the best by far. If these cost $50 or even $60 I'd be really happy with these, at least for sound. For $30 dollars I'm REALLY happy with them.

I'd be tempted to knock a star off for comfort but for me, the sound is everything so the 5 stars are for the sound.
text_fidelity_b: Shure SRH145m+ Portable Collapsible Headphones with Remote + Microphone Compatible with All Apple iOS Devices
